question: A communications team has two Claude-generated versions of a member newsletter and must choose one to develop further. Which two practices make that comparison reliable? Select two.
options: A) Ask Claude which of its two drafts is stronger and take that as the decision.
B) Choose the longer version, since more material means more can be cut later.
C) Score each version against the original brief instead of against the other one.
D) Write down the criteria that matter before either draft is read at all.
E) Choose the version that reads with more confidence and energy on first pass.
correct_answers: C) Score each version against the original brief instead of against the other one.
D) Write down the criteria that matter before either draft is read at all.
explanations: Claude has no access to the team's priorities beyond what was stated, so this outsources a judgment the communications team is better placed to make.
Length is not a proxy for quality. A longer draft may simply contain more filler, and cutting it back costs time the team need not spend.
Correct. Comparing each draft to the brief is a distinct safeguard: two versions can be ranked against each other while both fail the actual requirement.
Correct. Criteria set in advance stop the team from rationalising a preference formed while reading, which is the main way informal comparisons go wrong.
Confident writing is a style feature. It can accompany weaker content, and it is precisely the quality that makes an unreliable draft feel persuasive.
